You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
The snapshot looks like mid-2009, most likely June 2009.

- **Unemployment:** 8.9% with a 12-month rise of 3.9 points fits spring 2009. The rate was 8.7% in April and 9.4% in May, and 8.9% matches the March 2009 figure.
- **Equities:** US large-cap is up 26.1% over 3 months and down 32.2% over 12 months. The S&P low was in March 2009, so a 3-month gain of 26% points to roughly May–June 2009. The 12-month return of -32% fits May 2009 (May 2008 to May 2009 was about -29%). Emerging-market equity is up 56.6% over 3 months, which also fits.
- **Headline CPI:** -0.62% YoY fits mid-2009, since the trough was -2.1% in July 2009. April 2009 was -0.7% and May was -1.3%. That matches April better.
- **Core CPI:** 1.91% fits April 2009.
- **Fed funds rate:** 0.17% fits April 2009.
- **Industrial production:** -12.55% YoY fits April 2009.
- **VIX:** 31.67 at month-end April 2009 (it was about 32.9 on 30 April). Month-end May was about 28.
- **S&P monthly return:** the 1-month gain of +5.9% is April 2009 (+9.4%) or May 2009 (+5.3%). 3-month +26%, with March +8.5%, April +9.4% and May +5.3%, comes to about 25%. This matches May.
- **Dollar:** the +10.78% YoY change suggests a spring reading.
- **10-year yield:** 3.67% matches the end of May 2009 (about 3.5%) or end of April (about 3.1%), so it points to May or June.
- **Payrolls:** a 3-month average of -640k fits the period from March to May 2009.
- **Unemployment, again:** the 8.9% figure is the March value. A May snapshot would show 9.4%, so the data are likely as known at the end of April, with the April value of 8.9% (the first release was 8.9%).

Considering the unemployment, CPI, core CPI and payroll readings together, April 2009 fits the macro data best. The market data fit May better, though. For example, the 10-year yield rose 0.65 points over 3 months and the Treasury 1-month return was -2.2%. The 10-year was 2.69% at the end of February and 3.31% at the end of May, but 3.67% fits the end of June (3.53%). I settle on May 2009 as a compromise.
